newsitem.title: USA: U.S. HRW wheat in good shape, but threats loom.
newsitem.headline: U.S. HRW wheat in good shape, but threats loom.

text.p: The U.S. hard red winter wheat crop was in generally good condition, but agronomists warned Tuesday that dryness and disease could threaten the crop in coming weeks.

"So far, so good," said Rollie Sears, extension wheat breeder at Kansas State University (KSU) in Manhattan, Kansas. "We're just going to have to wait it out. There's lots of things looming on the horizon... Right now we're okay. It would just be nice to have a rain."
The lack of any significant precipitation since February in western Kansas has created low soil moisture levels that may pose a problem for dryland fields, Sears said.
"It's starting to get dry out west, especially in southwest (Kansas). There are some areas that are starting to show some significant stress -- some of the shallower soils out there," Sears said.

The National Weather Service's six- to 10-day weather outlook released Monday afternoon called for above-normal temperatures and normal to below-normal precipitation across much of the HRW wheat growing region.
Merle Witt, extension area agronomist for southwest Kansas, confirmed that the wheat in his area was in need of moisture soon, but he added that the crop was relatively disease- and insect-free.

"We do have subsoil moisture, which is often the larger problem to solve. We lack surface moisture ... so fields have a blueish cast to them rather than the good dark green color that we like to see," Witt said.
Witt said continued dryness could deprive the wheat of needed nutrients, thereby retarding spring growth.
Apart from the threat of damage from ongoing dryness, wheat still faces possible trouble from the spread of leaf rust, a fungal disease that can cause yield reductions.
Agronomists said leaf rust was increasing on wheat plants in Texas and Oklahoma, and the extent of any leaf rust epidemic will hinge on weather conditions over the next month.
Witt said leaf rust spores were likely present in Kansas, but dryness had so far prevented them from developing.
"(The spores) haven't infected the plant because it's been dry enough that there hasn't been enough moisture to germinate the spores at this point," Witt said.

Wayne Knox, a wheat grower in north central Texas, said rust had started to show up in the wheat in his area. He said that some of his fellow farmers had started to spray for wheat rust, although he had not.

Meanwhile, the weekly state crop reports, released Monday, showed that HRW wheat condition declined slightly in Oklahoma and Texas during the week ended Sunday, but remained mostly unchanged in Kansas.
Kansas wheat condition was rated 19 percent excellent, 68 good, 11 fair and two poor, compared to last week's rating of 20 percent excellent, 64 good, 13 fair and three poor.
Oklahoma wheat acreage was rated nine percent excellent, 70 good, 19 fair and two poor, compared to last week's rating of 13 percent excellent, 70 good, 15 fair and two percent poor.
Texas wheat acreage was rated 11 percent excellent, 46 good, 36 fair, six poor and one very poor, versus last week's 18 percent excellent, 40 good, 36 fair, five poor and one very poor.
